transcript:
Phil: What's your name?
Dawn: My name is Dawn Dickson. And I'm the founder and CEO of PopCom.
Jillian: Of - what is it called?
Dawn: PopCom.
Dawn: I was looking for a direct-to-customer distribution, so I looked at vending machines as a way to sell a retail product.
Dawn: Smart kiosks are popping up everywhere. Right now, there's eight million vending machines in the United States. One million of those are considered smart, which means they have a touch screen and they can accept credit cards. That number of smart machines is growing 30% year over year as retailers continue to bring new concepts into vending machines. So we’re targeting -
Dawn: From my experience in e-commerce, I got all of my information about my customer from tracking the IP address. I could tell the conversion rate from the IP, where they're located. I could re-market them, I could re-target them, I could send them an email thank you or say, "Hey, you abandoned your cart." But on the vending machines, there's no way to do that.
Dawn: I went out looking for a hardware solution and a software solution to sell products to customers on the spot, and it didn't exist. So we've developed a software solution that makes self-service retail smart. I said, "What is closest thing to a IP address in physical form?" And that's the human. That's the person. So we use anonymized –
Daniel: The customer.
Dawn: The customer. We use anonymized facial recognition at the point of sale to identify that customer.
Dawn: With the customer's permission, we can verify your face against your ID to dispense a product that's regulated. So think Sudafed, think cannabis, think -
Daniel: Alcohol.
Dawn: - alcohol. That you need an ID to verify. We have that ability.
Jillian: That's cool.
Dawn: So ultimately, the big vision is to be the data company that provides data about consumer retail purchases, demographic information, and the best place to put the next kiosk or vending machine based on the traffic. So we're purely data analytic software for self-service retail.
Dawn: Imagine this is a vending machine and you're walking up to it and shopping. So I'm gonna open up my camera because we’re gonna need the camera. I'm gonna stand in front of it so you can see that it's me, because it's looking, it's gonna look at my face. And this is... I'm gonna pick a pair of shoes. Again, very similar to the e-commerce experience.
Jillian: So you're assuming the pair of shoes is in the vending machine?
Dawn: This is what it sells. Customers, our customers can customize their interface to look like their website. So you're already comfortable, familiar, because this is what you're used to.
Daniel: Through your platform?
Dawn: Through my platform. I pick a size. I'm gonna add it to my cart. So I already entered my email. I have a discount, and there's my email, so I'm checking out.
Daniel: Yep.
Dawn: So I can pay. Let's say I'm gonna pay with face. I've already created an account. Let's say I've already created an account and pay with my face. And we're gonna pay with my face. Uh-oh. Pull it up again. Demo glitch. Okay.
Dawn: So the true functionality here, which I think I've turned my camera off somehow, this is the dashboard. So I'm the business. I just sold a pair of shoes. My camera was off. I have to do it again. I do this all the time, so let me just go to the analytics and show you that it actually does work.
Daniel: Do you... So your customer is the end retailer as opposed to the hardware owner?
Dawn: My customer, we have the vending machine and kiosk manufacturers, which we have - we have a partnership with the number one kiosk manufacturer in the country called Kiosk Information Systems, kiosk.com.
Jillian: You're only working with them right now?
Dawn: Currently, because I mean, we're –
Jillian: Because they're the biggest one and you figure -
Dawn: They're the biggest one. We wanna go to market with them.
Jillian: Yeah.
Dawn: We have a great relationship, and it's a great case study. If we're working with the number one in the country, who else is gonna tell us no?
Daniel: What is their market share?
Dawn: They're number one. They're number one manufacturer in the country.
Jillian: So what does that represent? Does that represent 50%? 60%?
Dawn: I actually don't have the numbers.
Daniel: The reason I'm asking is, is it - is this business predicated on, you know, one deal with that one –
Dawn: No, not at all.
Daniel: with kiosk.com? I think that actually could be a really good thing where, like, if you've locked up kiosk.com and they've got 90% market share, that's actually a great thing for you.
Jillian: Right.
Daniel: If they've got 5% market share and it's a completely fragmented market, you know, you're probably gonna have to do a bunch of these deals.
Dawn: You know, I don't know the number by heart. You know, I just…
Michael: And how do you charge for this?
Dawn: So we consider each vending machine to be its own store, because it is. And so we charge it - each base price is $200 per machine per month. We're also working to integrate with companies like Shopify so that we can actually, if you have a vending machine and a website, you can omnichannel manage your inventory, your messaging, your CRM all together.
Daniel: My biggest question here is, I think this only works if it generates value for the - for the brand. Like, for the end retailer.
Dawn: Definitely.
Daniel: Right? At the end of the day, like, that, that is your... Even though they're not paying you directly, that is the customer.
Dawn: That's who it's for.
Daniel: It's all about the retailer. It's all about the brand, the value.
Dawn: It's all about the retailer and the brand.
Daniel: So, so if... So let's start there, which is: what percent of sales, like, do these brands sell through this channel? And where I'm going with that is, you know, e-commerce analytics and physical retail analytics are valuable because that's where 99% of their sales are.
Dawn: Now. But think about in the '90s.
Daniel: So what, so what does that look like today for this channel? And are retailers kind of fine with not knowing that much about this channel just 'cause it's so immaterial?
Dawn: No, they're not fine. That's why we don't see as many machines in the United States selling physical products as we do in other countries like China and Japan -
Daniel: But just today.
Dawn: - where there's one machine for 20, every 23 people selling a product.
Daniel: I get that, but just today. So I get the what you need to believe story and I get that this is kind of an under-penetrated channel, but just today, if you take, um, that shoe brand, right, like what percent of their sales are done through this channel today?
Dawn: Not a lot because they don't have enough data to scale that business. So -
Daniel: Like 1%? 5%? .1%?
Dawn: Um, I honestly don't know that information.
Daniel: Cause that's really the critical question for me.
Dawn: So what I did to -
Daniel: Just to, just to make my point clear, I totally get, I get the value. I think it makes all the sense in the world. My, my hypothesis is there aren't a ton of retailers and brands that derive more than 1% of their revenue via this channel today –
Dawn: Because they don't have the opportunity.
Daniel: Hang on. Just today.
Dawn: Today.
Daniel: And so, um, if that's true, then I don't think that if - I don't think that if penetration just kind of stayed the same, that there'd be a business here because it's -
Dawn: It’s absolutely not gonna stay the same. It's growing 30% year over year.
Daniel: Okay, so that's, so, so that's the bet. So the bet is - we're betting on the fact that, you know, this channel will be 5, 10, 20% of these retailers' and brands' sales in 5, 10, 15 years from now.
Dawn: Yeah. We're betting on the fact that the $10 billion pop-up industry is going to continue to grow.
Daniel: Okay. I do think that the customer is... Like, you've obviously got, like, two customers, obviously. One, the, the manufacturer, and secondly, the end brand. And I, I do think - I think of the end brands and retailers as the most, obviously the most important part in this whole story because -
Dawn: It is the most important part.
Daniel: - they're the ones that are ultimately gonna determine your success.
Dawn: Absolutely.
Daniel: And so I still... And where I get caught up is I just don't know how important this channel is to them.
Dawn: So, like, in 1990, how important was e-commerce as a channel?
Daniel: Yeah. Yeah, it was zero.
Dawn: This is the future of retail.
Daniel: What makes you think that now is the time that this channel kind of inflects? Like, what are the forces that are coming together? E-commerce, you had - I mean, you used the example of e-commerce in the '90s and there was one big force, which is the internet.
Dawn: Yeah.
Daniel: Like, what is the force here?
Dawn: The force here is that, you know, brick and mortar's changing, but it's not going away. 82% of customer decisions are still made in stores. Customers just want more interactive experiences with brands like they're used to getting online. With the boom of the pop-up shops, it shows me that retailers online want a physical presence. They wanna connect with their customer in front of their customer and be selling products in real time, and the way to drive that would be through vending. I've watched the trends in other countries like Japan, like China, and like Europe, and seeing how automated retailing and self-service retail is growing.
Phil: Can you go - tell us your background?
Dawn: Yes. I've been an entrepreneur 16 years. I started my first tech company in 2001. I've never failed. None of my businesses ever failed. Got an acquisition offer, 50/50 partnership, didn't wanna sell. He kept it. I walked away. Started another venture -
Jillian: Wait, back up.
Dawn: - a consulting company.
Phil: Yeah.
Jillian: Back up. Back up. Back up.
Dawn: It's long. It's 16 years' worth. You want me -
Jillian: Well, you can just tell. Um, so 2001, you built a company. That was what type of company?
Dawn: A media company. So we were streaming video before YouTube, streaming music platform.
Daniel: Cool.
Dawn: It was a website for entertainment and events in central Ohio. We had the first of its kind website. We had the first email list in the city. We were getting over 100,000 unique visits and hits every month locally. And -
Phil: And how did you exit that?
Dawn: I just walked away from it and let my partner keep it. He didn't wanna sell it, and he's still doing it. So -
Phil: You - Why did you walk away?
Dawn: I wanted to do something else.
Jillian: So didn't you sell percentage of, didn't you sell your -
Dawn: No, I still have - I still have my same ownership. He just –
Jillian: Oh, okay.
Phil: You still own half of it?
Dawn: Yeah.
Jillian: Oh, okay.
Dawn: He just does his thing with it, and he's turning it into a app now. And -
Phil: Okay, so what'd you do after that?
Dawn: Started a consulting company in 2005 to then help businesses do what I did and grow their online following. So I did that for five years, and then I gave my book of business to another consultant. Just exited that one, too. So, um, small little buyout. It wasn't, like, an official exit. And then I started a consumer product company.
Phil: And?
Dawn: And grew that business. Um, started that 2011. That is the business that I showed you with the shoes. I started selling shoes in vending machines in Atlanta Airport, in Club Liv and the Fontainebleau Hotel, MGM Grand in Las Vegas. I wanted to scale that business. I couldn't scale it without data. And then I got the idea for this business.
Phil: So did you shut that business down?
Dawn: I did not shut that business down. I hired a COO to run it, and I stepped down from the business, but I'm still -
Jillian: It's one of your customers.
Dawn: It's one of my customers.
Jillian: Right.
Dawn: My first customer. My first paying customer.
Jillian: What's it called? Flat? Flat?
Dawn: Flat Out Of Heels. So my business is my first paying customer.
Daniel: Oh, that's cool.
Daniel: So, um, here's where I stand. I think, um... So I guess where we agree is I think this solution makes a ton of sense for the brands and retailers. Like, it just seems like they should get the same level of data inside analytics as they do in all the other channels that they're in. So I get the pain, I guess, and I get the solution. Like, that all checks off. I think where I might disagree with you is I just think, you know, like retail, US retail is, like, this big elephant, and I feel like this channel is, like, an ant. So I just feel like the easy way out for these brands and for most brands and retailers is to kinda say, "Hey, this is, like, less than 1%, less than half a percent of our sales, and so I don't really, like, care or need analytics on this channel." And so for that, for those reasons, I think you're building a great product, I just kinda can't get there on market size, so I'm gonna pass.
Dawn: Let me just give you a - real quick, before -
Daniel: Yeah.
Dawn: Let's just say, okay, you're right. You're right. Only 20,000 vending machines want this. At 200 a month, that's a good business.
Daniel: It's an okay business.
Dawn: It's a pretty good business.
Daniel: Yeah.
Dawn: I mean, 20,000 at 200 a month's base. But that's not the case. But I just wanna give you a perspective. And also, you remind me of, like, the people in the '90s who said, "We don't need a website to sell our products. We don't... We don't... We're not gonna sell online. We're doing good in the store."
Daniel: Yeah, but I just... I guess, um, not to belabor the point, I don't see the growth catalyst here for the channel. Whereas in e-commerce in the '90s, it was the internet. So, like, what is that now? Besides -
Dawn: It's the convenience. It's, you know, again, you see the airport kiosk, you see the movie theater, the restaurant kiosk. All these kiosks can use our software to understand who their customers are. The software can be used on those kiosks -
Daniel: Yeah
Dawn: - same as they can to buy a product. Doesn't have to be just to buy a product. It could be to transact.
Daniel: Yeah.
Dawn: So you're out, but when you walk out the door and go places, start to look at how many kiosks you see.
Daniel: Yeah.
Dawn: Everywhere. There's not a place without a kiosk. There's not a place.
Daniel: Yeah. You look torn, Jillian.
Jillian: I'm so torn, I can't stand it.
Daniel: What are you torn, what, what are you -
Jillian: You wanna know why I'm torn? Is because I don't really invest in areas I don't know anything about. But I'm not a big shopper, and so I don't have that experience of - I don't think I'd ever buy anything out of a kiosk because I don't know if I have that trust. I couldn't buy a pair of shoes out of a kiosk. What if it comes out? So there is a level of trust. The same thing with makeup. What if it's old and I, you know, I can't see it, and I can't open it, and I don't have that trust? So me, personally, I don't get, I don't understand the whole kiosk sell. I get it's an expanding business. I believe you, and the fact that I see pop-up shops, and I definitely see that this is going to be a very vital piece of the retail, this sort of hybrid, all right? I see these vending machines all over Europe, all over, right, Asia, and I agree with you. We're behind. We're behind. If I had this acumen, I would invest in this, but I don't, and so I add zero value and, in fact, I think would be one of the, like, the dumb investors that have all the stupid questions and would just use up a lot of your time. And for that reason, I'm gonna pass.
Phil: Um, so I, I agree with Jillian that I feel like you're sort of riding a wave, and I think that I'm a little less concerned with sort of the percentage of sales that are currently done through this channel because I think it's just gonna grow very quickly. You know, I think that the younger generations, younger people in this country are becoming more and more accustomed to using facial - facial recognition for payment, for transactions. So I really like the product. I really do, and I like the market even though it's sort of at its nascent stage. Where I'm struggling is, well, I don't, I don't love the sort of the distribution channel. I'm a believer in having control of your own destiny and sort of selling it yourself as opposed to relying on a partner like the manufacturer to sell it. So that's a concern. I mean, it's tempting because I feel like, you know, you're at a - you're not raising much, but I really would like to see you make the first tweaks to the system, which you'll make after you get feedback. I'd like to get to that next stage. So I feel like for me, I would be extremely interested in the next round and –
Dawn: Awesome.
Phil: Or even if this round is open when you're still generating revenue, which it probably won't be, but if it is, I'd be interested in that.
Michael: So I would say that I thought you were a little, uh, the way you kind of talked about your history, about giving away this company here and there, and that, it threw me off a little bit as an investor. Cause my immediate gut, and I know it was theirs, was did you just give away money, and how are you gonna treat our money? So just be careful about your history.
Jillian: I agree with that.
Michael: You know? Right?
Jillian: I did agree with that.
Michael: And I, and I just wanna know that, we always wanna know that our money's treated like yours.
Jillian: That you're not gonna just
Phil: Michael, that, that was a red flag for me. Hearing about your history and the three ventures and -
Michael: It was dismissive.
Jillian: And that you just walked away.
Phil: That was a red flag.
Jillian: That’s a concern.
Michael: Yeah. So, so maybe frame that in a different way.
Dawn: I will. Yeah. Thank you.
Michael: But you are, you are really smart, and you got this thing nailed down. And actually, you were such a machine gun at the beginning of this pitch, I'm like, "What? We're gonna ask a question. We're not gonna stump this entrepreneur." And, and you did a great job. I have a tough time believing a few things. I have a tough time believing the 200 bucks cause that's a lot of money for a vending machine. I have a tough time believing that no one's done any of this kind of stuff in advanced places like Japan and Korea, and places that are 10 years ahead by your own admission, and Europe, who are much better at this stuff. In saying that, I do think vending machines will get a lot more advanced, and a lot more AI will come in, and yeah, let's throw it in there, maybe the blockchain will connect it all and make a ledger of what's being sold, and everything you're doing data, 'cause it's the -
Daniel: Wow, you went there.
Michael: Yeah, you have to. You gotta throw in AI and blockchain to everything if you want up your valuation. I'm kinda sitting where Phil is. I would like to pay a higher valuation for your company, and I'd like to put in more money when you have 500 or 1,000 vending machines, and I'd like to pay for that right. I'd like to pay a 10, 15, $20 million valuation when you have actual real revenue, and you're proving that the dogs are eating the dog food, the people are drinking the champagne. That's where this thing would be for me.
